seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Manuscripts and Archives Division, New York Public Library

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
My dear editor: A line to wish you a happy New Year and to thank you for £10 received. I suppose you have now the first and second episodes. The third will follow in a week or so and I daresay the three will carry you over three months. I cannot get more typed or more quickly as my typist has not much free time. Typing is also an expense. I calculate the typing expenses of Ulysses at £20 or £25. Possibly I shall cover this by sale of the MS. e così una mano lava l’altra . I am much obliged by your kindness and that of Miss Weaver 's in advancing money to me on an unseen MS. I had a letter some time ago from a Mrs M’Cormick who is staying in the Hotel Baur au Lac, Zurich. She is, I hear, a daughter of Mr Rockefeller. At her request I sent her a copy of Exiles
. I shall write you a letter in a day or two.

postscript.p: P.S. On p. 8 of second episode please read “baited” for “bated” in both copies.

note.p: Pound was serving as foreign editor of the New York magazine The Little Review, edited by Margaret Anderson and Jane Heap. As JJ finished the early episodes in Locarno, he sent them off to Zurich to be typed; typed copies were then sent to Pound in London who reviewed and passed a copy on to New York for printing in The Little Review. Clare Hutton observes that JJ “required three typed copies … one to keep for future reference, one for Pound, and the third either for Weaver and The Egoist [which published a few episodes of Ulysses], or for onward submission to the Little Review” (Hutton, Serial Encounters: Ulysses and The Little Review [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019], 87). It is clear from the postscript in this postcard, however, that Pound had been sent two copies (“both copies”).

After receiving “Telemachus,” the first episode of Ulysses, Pound wrote JJ of his enthusiasm on 19 December 1917: “I think it is the only youth that has ever been written down.” Then he lapsed into stage backwoods-American, a persona he often adopted to cover strong emotion: “Wall, Mr. Joice, I recon your a damn fine writer, that’s what I recon’. An’ I recon’ this here work o’ yourn is some concarn’d litterchure. You can take it from me, an’ I’m a jedge” (Pound/Joyce 128-29).

div.note: Presumably payment from Pound as foreign editor of The Little Review for the first episodes of Ulysses, following through on Pound’s hope, expressed in his letter of 19 December 1917, to “forward a few base sheckles in a few days time” (Pound/Joyce 129).

In Locarno, JJ was finishing the first three episodes of Ulysses – “Telemachus,” “Nestor,” and “Proteus” – and sending them off to Zurich to be typed, thence to be transmitted to Pound. “Telemachus” was sent to Pound circa 12 December 1917 (LI 110). Pound had thought that “Telemachus,” running to seventeen pages in typescript, might be broken into three installments for The Little Review (Pound/Joyce 129), but the episode appeared entire in the number for March 1918. “Nestor” and “Proteus” were printed in the numbers for April and May 1918, respectively.

As JJ finished each episode in Locarno, he sent it to his British friend, the professional actor Claud W. Sykes (1883-1964), for typing in Zurich. Sykes had been given the loan of a typewriter for the job by Rudolf Goldschmidt (1880-1975), a grain merchant in Zurich who was a friend and pupil of JJ. Goldschmidt had married a Triestine woman, Gemma Weiss (1891-1970), in 1913. Gemma was the sister of Ottocaro Weiss (1896-1971), a student at the University of Zurich and close friend of JJ and his family. Another sibling was Paula or Paola Weiss (1900-1990), who may have inspired JJ to give Leopold Bloom his middle name of Paula (U 17.1855; Ellmann, JJ 464).

JJ remitted to Claud Sykes, for typing the Ulysses episodes, a money order for “20 francs in advance as per our agreement” in November 1917 (LI 108) and further payments of 10 francs and 4 francs in December (LII 413, 415).

note.p: It. “And so one hand washes the other” (or “You scratch my back and I scratch yours”), an expression suggesting that mutual favors are being performed – here, the notion that the costs of typescript will be covered by sums given for manuscript. The New York lawyer John Quinn (1870-1924), a collector of modern art and literary manuscripts, had been purchasing items from JJ, including the manuscript of his play Exiles and the setting copy used for the American edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) (see JJ to Pound, 19 March 1917, notes, and 24 July 1917, notes).

As JJ anticipates in this postcard, Quinn later inquired, in a letter to JJ of 26 June 1919, if he could purchase the autograph manuscript of Ulysses; and on 5 February 1920 he cabled JJ an advance of 3,000 lire or $153.85, and on 15 August 1920 another advance of 3,400 francs or $250, with an additional payment of 1,400 francs in the fall of 1920 (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 237, 241-42, 245-46, 254, 258). The manuscript ran to 1,200 pages (Library of John Quinn, pt. 1 [New York: Anderson Galleries, 1923], 487). JJ was irritated when Quinn later sold it along with other items from his library (Ellmann, JJ 558).

div.note: In a letter to Nora Barnacle dated 10 September 1917, Pound mentioned that JJ should have received “£10 telegraphed by the Egoist,” which was planning to publish episodes of Ulysses in London, and he hoped to pay him £50 or more, in due course, for the work’s serialization in The Little Review in New York (Pound/Joyce 125-26). After receiving the typescript of “Telemachus,” Pound wrote JJ on 19 December 1917, “Hope to forward a few base sheckles in a few days time” (Pound/Joyce 129).

Mrs. Harold McCormick (Edith Rockefeller) (1872-1932) was the daughter of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller. She was a Chicago patron of the arts and of psychoanalysis who lived in Zurich during World War I and contributed generously to the Psychological Club there. She financed translations of C.G. Jung into various languages and established a foundation to patronize writers, musicians, and artists. She spontaneously gifted JJ a stipend of 1,000 Swiss francs per month from March 1918 through September 1919, when she just as suddenly terminated the benefaction (LII 453-54). Her abrupt change of mind may have had to do with JJ’s refusal to be psychoanalyzed by Jung (Ellmann, JJ 422-23, 466-69).

JJ had recently corrected proof on Exiles and the play was published on 25 May 1918. He may here be referring to a typescript copy of the work: in late November 1917, for example, he had instructed James Pinker to lend “the other typescript” (LII 410) to the Stage Society for consideration. It is also possible that JJ is referring to a dedication copy and Exiles is a slip for A Portrait. He had inscribed a copy of the Egoist Portrait to McCormick on 19 December 1917; a copy of Exiles would follow, inscribed on 30 May 1918.

In the “Nestor” episode of Ulysses – typescript of which had been sent to Pound from Zurich circa 27 December 1917 (LI 110) – Stephen Dedalus, working as a teaching assistant in a private school, hears the clamor of the schoolboys playing hockey in the yard and is put in mind of savage combat: “a shout of spearspikes baited with men’s bloodied guts” (Little Review, vol. 4, no. 12 [April 1918]: 41; U 2.318).
